items.18: Good morning everyone. In the past, we would get a post, and that carries. You have speakers on the agenda here today. Before we get to that, anybody declaring a conflict of interest here today? Not seeing any. And if I get somebody to move the minutes. Councillor Holly Kelleher. General Manager of Community Services, and if I may, Mr. Chair, I'd like to draw the committee's attention to a change in the recommendation for this report before you. The Planning and Development and Community Services Committee has delegated authority to approve the grants outlined in this report. Therefore, the recommendation has been updated. It will now be that the Standing Policy Committee on Planning and Development and Community Services approve the cash grants totaling $630,600 under the Social Services Category Assistance to Community Groups Grant Program, as outlined in this report from the Community Services Division dated May 6, 2020. Ms. Leslie Anderson, Director of Planning and Development, will be introducing this report. Great. Thank you. Good morning. The Social Assistance Cash Grant Award is a grant program adjudicated by the Social Services Subcommittee of Council. The members of the Subcommittee are noted in the report. The Chair of the Subcommittee is here, and I'd like to thank them all for their time and for participating in the process. The Subcommittee reviews applications from non-profit social service agencies, pursuant to Council Policy CO3-018, assistance to community groups, ensuring that the objectives of the policy are met. The 2020-26 assistance to community groups grant program, Social Services Category, is administered as part of the Saskatoon Collaborative Funders Partnership as well. This is a collaboration between two Saskatoon organizations that provide grants to community groups. The Associated Grants are the City of Saskatoon Social Services Grant and the United Way Community Initiatives' Fund. This collaboration helps both funders make stronger decisions in the programs and also simplifies the application process for the group applying for funding. Non-profits and federally registered charities are eligible under the program, and the Council Policy provides for the applications to be judged based on the degree to which they demonstrated community need, aiming to impact the largest number of people in the community. Applications are considered in categories of services to families, including youth and children, services to seniors, and health and rehabilitation services. Based on the subcommittee's review, they're recommending funding support to 29 agencies in Saskatoon to be provided via these cash grants. And with that, with the noted change in the recommendation, I can take any questions or come back after the speakers. Great. Not seeing any questions at this time. We'll go right to speakers. From what I've heard from a Sanger, we have checked signing authority for this committee today, so it's not going to Council, so that's good. I'll call Shantel Johnson to come to the podium. Ms. Johnson, and for all speakers, you have five minutes to address this here today. You're going to hear a loud screech once you get to that end point. Any time you're ready, introduce yourself and who you're representing, if there is anyone. And that would be great. Yes, thank you. Thank you for agreeing to hear me this morning, and good morning, Councillors, on this hopefully spring morning on Treaty 6 territory and homeland of the Métis. My name is Shantel Johnson, and I've had the privilege of being the Executive Director of CLASS for the last 14 years. For those of you who may not be aware, CLASS stands for Community Legal Assistance for Saskatoon in our City. We're Saskatchewan's only community legal clinic, and we're situated in Saskatoon, your city. We provide a myriad of services, including full legal representation, summary advice to unrepresented folks, community support work, which is social work and systems navigation, ID clinics, and student training. My focus on CLASS today will be on our full legal representation clinic and on our community support work, because that's where our service contract between the City and the United Way through the collaborative funders has been focused. Last fiscal year, ending March 31st, CLASS worked on 1,175 client files, benefiting way more than just those individuals because children are often involved, and we denied 179 files due to capacity with four lawyers on staff. Through our community support work program, what we originally thought would happen was that we would be doing a lot of referrals, but what we've learned through experience is that it's actually a lot of full-on case support because of the dire situation a lot of our community members are facing. We're really proud that we were started by students from the ground up, and they're really intentional about all the words that we know now, reconciliation, decolonization, before those were words that were in the common vernacular. But this isn't only about CLASS this morning; this is about all of the other non-profits that you've funded, too. Non-profits do some of community's most difficult work and fill gaps in services. We keep community safe. We promote social justice through food security, literacy, education, employment training, social services, and other system navigation, and municipalities benefit from them because we're in your cities. Non-profits matter locally because they reduce strain on public systems and reach vulnerable populations quickly and effectively. And this has been demonstrated recently by the loss of a community agency that's impacted both the city and our agencies. Why are social grants critical? They invest in your community; they can provide stability depending on process. Impact: they may allow non-profits to sustain or expand programming. Efficiencies: non-profits are a cost-effective way of delivering services and prevent higher downstream costs. Leverage ability: often, if a municipality will invest in an agency that's seen in high regard by other funders. I'm going to focus on CLASS just a little bit for our full legal representation clinic. Our files span from wills to powers of attorney, refugee law, housing law, criminal, human rights, social services, and beyond. I'll give you a couple of typical client stories. One, most recently, was an Indigenous woman who took the brave step of moving down from up north with her little girl, two years old. She came to us, not when her heating stopped, but when the oven stopped, because the landlord had told her to just open the oven and turn it on to heat her basement suite by SAS Polytech. She was at risk because she then developed health issues and had missed some school. She was at risk of failing out of SAS Polytech. We dealt with the landlord matter through the Office of Residential Tenancies, but we also helped advocate at SAS Polytech and explain what had been going on to get the absenteeism policy waived. And this demonstrates some of the downstream effects of housing that lots of people don't think about. Once your housing is precarious, you're oftentimes at risk of losing employment, losing your education, and having sick children. Another really common thing we're seeing lately, in fact our highest area of demand, is refugee and immigration law. Last year, the last two years, in fact, it surpassed housing law. Lots of people are fleeing their home countries due to risk of persecution, political affiliation, and religion, among other things. These are the tensions we're now facing: balancing between our originally intended clients and our newcomer clients. I see I have 21 seconds. Social return on investment in places such as CLASSIC, research demonstrates it's either $6-$7 to $10 saved when you invest in clinics such as CLASSIC. So I'd like to thank the city for your social investment, and I'd like to urge you to continue to do so. Three seconds, nailed it. Perfect. I'm just going to hold you for two seconds. You might have a question for you, just give me two seconds. So we do have one, or we have a couple actually. Councillor Senos Timon: Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Through you, Councillor Troy Davies. Thank you, Mr. Johnson, for your presentation and for the good work you and all your team are doing in the community. My question is about the intake process. Can you help me understand the intake process and the income requirements? What income level would one qualify for the services? Yes, we do have income eligibility, but unlike legal aid, we don't publish it because we don't have the administrative capacity to take all of the forms, tax receipts, and everything. So our income eligibility is higher than legal aid's; it's more akin to the low-income cut-off line. People can work, often are working low-income jobs, and can own property sometimes. We also have discretion around that, so it's higher than legal aid, where you have to basically be in receipt of public assistance to qualify, but not that high, kind of akin to the low-income cut-off. So what's the low-income cut-off? Well, it depends on the number of children and dependents in the family. I think it starts at about $1,200 and goes up to about $4,600 a month, depending on dependents. So there's flexibility in terms of income. Yes, and other considerations are made around assets as well. Okay, thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you for the work that you do, but thank you also for your comments on non-profits in general. I was just sitting here grinning when you were speaking, because it's 100% true: they're more efficient, they're more effective, they reach people on the ground much better than we can as a municipality. So I appreciate your giving the flowers to the full non-profit community. Just curious, you talked about the two topics, but immigration, you said, is the rising issue that you have at CLASSIC. I'm wondering if it's been impacted at all due to the federal cuts on immigration funding, or are those kind of in line with each other, or is that just because we're having those higher immigration movements? I think that the numbers you're seeing at CLASSIC are specifically because we have a legal aid system that hasn't historically practiced in refugee or immigration law in Saskatchewan. We're one of only a few. We will get a bit of reprieve as others are going to start doing some of that law in the coming year. We've been on an advisory panel with them about that. We're not sure what they'll do because of their income cut-off. We're afraid that a lot of the folks that we currently work with would get kicked off their services immediately upon getting refugee status when you get a work permit, because then they're working. So we're working through all of those things with them, but I think it's more to do with the fact that we don't have any other free legal service providers in this city and in this province who work in immigration and refugee. More than anything, we are being impacted by some changes at the federal level right now that make refugee applications more difficult. So it's requiring a lot more quick work done at the front end, as you know, social policy changes always affect people applying law on the ground. No, I appreciate that. The other one that you brought up was housing. Obviously, it's the number one issue we deal with in chambers here; we talk about it a lot. I'm just curious, what are the general issues that come to you when it comes to folks in housing? So you gave us an example of something that's particularly egregious, but I'm just curious, what types of issues do you see? I think the three main issues will be landlords that are being really exploitative. We have clients that are being asked to live in garden sheds, asked to live without utilities, asked to provide sex for rent, and so advocating where people do have landlords on the other end of things with that community support work I talked about. The primary work that the social worker does is to try to find people housing. It's incredibly difficult on income assistance numbers right now, and so a lot of times what we're also doing is just safety planning with our community members, providing for daily check-ins for proof of life. Because that's where we've come in the 14 years I've been at CLASSIC: a lot of folks simply cannot find housing, and so it's around safety planning around housing. So it's a spectrum of dealing with folks who do have housing but maybe landlord issues, habitability issues, all the way to people who absolutely can't find housing because of the income that they're on and the private market that we're relying on for housing right now. I think it sounds like you're a mirror for the issues and the gaps that we're seeing in Saskatoon in our housing spectrum. Well, thank you very much for being here today. I appreciate it. Thank you. I think that's it. Thank you very much. Okay. Thanks. Next, we have Cheryl Harrow Yurak. Sorry. Thanks for your indulgence. Sorry. We had another piece. Do you have another question? Oh, sorry. I just wanted to alert everyone that we're having some technical difficulties with the camera that's facing the podium; it's glitching out. So we're trying to adjust the camera for anybody watching on the feed. If you see that we're not having the cameras on the podiums for a long term, it's just because the feed is technically glitching out. Just wanted to let everybody know. Okay. Okay. Perfect. Anytime you're ready, I'm going to introduce this, and then we'll hear what's going to be done. Thank you. The record, I'm fine with the camera glitching out. No issue there. I can live stream you from here. No, stop it. I just want to start by saying thank you very much for this opportunity and also Shantel. Your work is so important to our community, and we are honored as an organization to work closely with you and the people that you serve. Your staff are spectacular and also so accountable; thank you for everything. Good morning, everyone. My name is Cheryl, and I'm the Executive Director of Foundations Learning, formerly Reed Saskatoon, so that may ring a bell with you. We've been in the community for nearly 50 years now. We are a non-profit charitable organization located on Duchess, and we love our location, but our lease is up at the end of June, and I can tell you finding a new home for a non-profit these days is not easy. For those of you that are new to us, Foundations Learning works across Saskatoon to build practical skills for life. That includes reading, writing, money management, digital skills, and family learning, so people can move forward with confidence. We work with adults who want to read to their children for the first time, with newcomers navigating a new country, with parents who want to give their kids the best possible start, and with people who face real barriers, not because they lack ability or ambition, but because life got in the way of learning. Our programs are free; our volunteers are our neighbors, and some of you in this room as well, which is very much appreciated. Last year we had 315 volunteers, which is the equivalent of about 18 full-time staff, who serve and work one-on-one and address the mission and vision of our organization. Our work is only possible because of the community and investments that we receive, majority... are through donations and through the City of Saskatoon, so thank you very much. The City's cash grants program, and us as a flagship organization, has been the support since 2006 to our organization, and you help ensure that our programs are free. With that, we can match volunteer literacy coaches to work one-on-one with adults who are strengthening their reading, writing, and numeracy skills. We are also very grounded in outcomes, and we know that 98% of the adults that we serve improve those skills. Last year, we worked with 636 individuals who attended our financial literacy workshops: things like managing debt and credit, budgeting, learning information about filing taxes, and actually filing taxes as well. That's a new program that we launched this year. And after participating in our programs, participants reported that 90% of them follow a budget more carefully after being a part of our program, and 63% take steps to repair their credit. Debt is a real fear for many of the people that we serve, and it's so easy to get credit these days and get yourself in trouble. We reach families through programs that build the home as a place of learning, and our volunteers make a significant difference. But none of this happens without stable local funding, so I want to thank you very much for that. The City's investment in community organizations isn't just a line item; it is the infrastructure of a caring community. When you fund organizations like Classic or like ours, you're not funding one program; you're funding a network of groups that are committed to the health of our community and to the individuals that struggle the most to succeed. We work alongside library schools, newcomer-serving organizations, social services agencies, health care partners, and in fact, last year we worked with 300 organizations to do our work. We share referrals, we meet for lunch, we talk about our challenges, and we help offset each other's heavy burdens at times. The collaboration is only possible when each organization in that ecosystem is stable and well-resourced. Pulling one thread weakens the web for all of us, as we have just witnessed. The people who come to Foundations Learning are often the same people who are navigating food insecurity, housing instability, and limited income. Eighty percent of the 5,000 people that we serve earn less than $30,000 a year. Most of them rent or couch-surf; many are striving for better goals and hopes for their family, and sometimes they're just stuck. Our job as community organizations is to help them find a way through, as no single organization can meet this need. Thank you. Are there any questions for our speaker? Councillor Kelleher. Thank you, and through you, Chair Davies. My question was a little bit around how the agencies work together, so I think I'll maybe just pick up where you left off. When we talk about the investments that are made into not-for-profits and into social programming, and Shantel, you may have comments on this as well, could you talk a little bit about it? It seems like there's a bit more of an exponential effect when you take into account how all the agencies actually work together to serve clients. Could you speak a little bit to navigating and how you may work among yourselves for referrals and pieces like that? I'm assuming that happens. It does, and in fact, a lot of it is an infrastructure piece for each organization. So for example, within our four program areas, we have a program manager. For financial literacy, they attend community meetings like the Poverty Reduction Strategy. They are networked with staff, so for example, with Classic, referrals need to happen. We know, because we sit at that Poverty Reduction meeting forum, that we can make referrals directly because the one important part about community work is that it is relationship-based. So it's not about referring people from organization to organization; it's about referring from person to person. For example, I can say, "You need to go talk to Shantel," or "Can I get Shantel on the phone to talk to you?" And that's what the staff in each organization does as well. The relationships between organizations are imperative; the relationships between staff to staff are imperative as well. Thank you. I think that's it. Thank you very much. So, a little bit up to committee, are there any questions for administration? Not seeing any. We do have one recommendation on the floor, so I'm going to be willing to move that, Councillor Kelleher. So I'll call a question. Any opposed? And that carries 6.2.3, Ms. Anchor.
items.24:
Good morning, everybody. It's an honor for me to come here today and put forth what I was asked to do for our elders. As you know, we had meetings regarding the naming of the province of the people here that are sitting. Unfortunately, there was a lot of hard work. A lot of the elders worked, and a lot of them were unable to come because most of them were in wheelchairs and different things. And of course, they nominated that I must be the most. So here I am. I just want to say I'm a mature woman. I was born and raised here all my life. I just turned 88 years of age. I never thought I'd be standing in City Hall and talking to you people. I'm concerned for what happened there at that time. There was a lot of good work, a lot of hard work for our elders. Not only that, we had some young people, and I'm always there for young people. I was very impressed to hear the voices of our young people and also our elders. So they made that decision that they would like to call it Sunshine. And the reason for that is traditionally, it was a traditional way of our way of life as we were growing up from the old people. And this was very important to them. When they left there, they were kind of feeling disappointed because they thought there were so many that were there, and they all made their own decisions. But at that time, I said to them, you know, there were a lot of different names that came out. So we looked at them, and that decision was made. We're hoping that new people will look at that and then give us that opportunity as Indigenous people, especially our people and our young people. So I come here today and speak on behalf of them and for our young people. Of course, I'm concerned about that, and I'd like to see that continued on. We had a meeting; I met with them, and it's now back here. So I hope by the time I get back to tell my fellow elders that we've made some progress. And I think it's important that we as Indigenous people have a say and we come back to our City Hall. And I want to say, teaching everyone, I hope I'm not going to go on. I can do a lot at the time. But I was a Road Allowance child. I was born and lived in a Road Allowance, and so in Nutana. And here, I was a woman at collegiate in 1953. And you know, when I look back and see me being able to talk, I can remember these old people were always worried to go out into the real world. So actually, I was one that was picked to look after the old people, and I had to take them out. So I've been around the city for many, many years and got to know people. And also be able to live and work with not only Aboriginal people, but all people. I work with many people here. So my voice is what I came to hear, and hopefully, when I leave here, that we'll take some interest in what I'm saying. I think it's important that our people have this. Some of the land is ours as well. And I really feel it's important that it should be undertaken. Thank you.

Councillor Parker: Thank you very much for being here today. It's always an honor to hear you speak, so I appreciate you bringing your words and the words of your fellow elders. I'm just curious, can you clarify? So this name came up through a process, and I certainly appreciate everybody that took part in that process. I'm just curious why the name that's being recommended today is in English.

Good morning. Dorsey. I swiffle. I have taken part in the meetings, and I'm here to support. The reason why the name Sunshine was in English was that we... We just need you to speak into the mic there, and if you can just introduce yourself.

Don't cut me off then. Good morning. Dorsey. I swiffle. I had the opportunity and the honor to take part in the naming, picking the names for the new area. And the reason why Sunshine was chosen was because when we are in ceremony, we do things with sunrise, at sunrise. But we also wanted an English name, as well as all the languages of Saskatoon on a plaque. So that way, it shows that we are working together as a community and in reconciliation. So that's why the old people chose Sunshine and English, with the understanding that the other languages would be recognized and be put on the plaque as well. Right. I hope that answers your question. That's great. Thank you very much. Any other questions?

Councillor Timon: Thank you. I just want to say thank you, Elder, for your wisdom and leadership in the community. For the first several years that I've gotten to know you, I meet you in the community and witness the work that you're doing and the care you're giving, especially amplifying the voices for young ones. It's very inspiring. I want to say thank you for the leadership to all the participants. I was very amazed with the process, how the name came up through those five ceremonies on the process. You know, everyone batting different names. Excuse me. Everyone batting different names and then going through the process of, 'Okay, let us select from this name.' But there's something that came, not really from the process of that five ceremonies. I just say thank you for sharing that and having the process in a very thoughtful way that shared the name that also represents everybody, not only Indigenous but really encompassed who we are as a community. So I just want to say thank you so much.

And I'm going to open up to committee for administration. Ms. Anger, do you want to provide any high-level briefing before we open up the questions for committee?

Yes. Thank you, Mr. Chair. So the item before committee is a letter from the Office of the City Clerk concerning a recommendation from the Civic Naming Committee related to the naming of the University Heights three neighborhood. And I would like to invite Richard Phillips, the Chief Strategy and Transformation Officer, who will introduce this item further and walk through the process from the Civic Naming Committee.

Richard Phillips: Good morning. Richard Phillips, Chief Strategy and Transformation Officer here at the City of Saskatoon. Thank you for having me. Through the Chair to the committee, I'm here to share an update on legacy naming and the University Heights three neighborhood, specifically. I'll talk a bit about a review of the Civic Naming Committee, its history, an update on the University Heights three neighborhood naming process, future naming requests, and some next steps. Next slide, please. First, I'd like to share a brief history of the creation and mandate of the committee, as well as current policy for the naming of civic property. Next slide. Before you, you see a slide of a timeline with milestones related to the Civic Naming Committee. The green items represent decisions, and the orange items represent information updates that were taken forward. Moving left to right, you'll see that in June 2018, the Civic Naming Committee was created. In June 2021, a request was made to rename John A. McDonald Road. In December 2022, the Legacy Naming Project budget was approved. And in August and September of 2023, Council approved the renaming of John A. McDonald Road. In June 2024, there was a request to provide lessons learned, a place identity framework, and revisions to the existing policy. In May 2025, two of those items were completed, as the lessons learned were received as information, and the place identity framework was approved. The last two items on this slide, I'll speak to in more detail in a future section. In June 2018, the Naming Advisory Committee was renamed to the Civic Naming Committee. Its terms of reference and policy were approved. In March 2018, Council resolved that the CNC managed and organized the names master list. Administration assigned names to city-owned properties, and updates to the policy needed to be made.

The mandate of the Civic Naming Committee was as follows: review requests for names and manage the names master list; work with administration to organize the names master list into themes and prioritize the names for selection; and finally, work with the Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Advisory Committee to find ways to increase the number of names on the list. The CNC is comprised of three members of Council, at least four members of administration, and one member sitting on both the Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Advisory Council and the Civic Naming Committee.

The current policy is outlined as follows: Name requests are received by our Planning and Development Division. Those names are presented to the CNC. If a name is accepted at that time, administration prioritizes the name and places it in a theming area. The CNC receives and reviews an updated list and recommends that the committee approve the new list.

The Legacy Review Project had three outcomes: lessons learned from the renaming of John A. Macdonald and the process that was used; an update to the existing naming policy; and the development of a Place Identity Framework. In May 2024, the lessons learned and the Place Identity Framework items were completed, but the updates to the current policy are still outstanding.

The approved Place Identity Framework recognized that the current policy was not inclusive of all residents that the City of Saskatoon serves. As part of the approved framework, the following changes were identified to be made: separate the process for gathering names from the process for applying names; appoint community members to the Civic Naming Committee; and target inclusion percentages for the names on the list from Indigenous, newcomer, and marginalized communities in Saskatoon, as well as defining a process for modifying or removing names from the list if required.

Another shared item was the history of the Civic Naming Committee and the existing policy. I'd like to provide an update on the process for naming the University Heights 3 neighborhood. Specifically, I shared information related to a previous request for administration for guidance as it relates to the naming process; information related to the previous updates on UH3 to the Civic Naming Committee; information on a targeted engagement process; and finally, several recommendations from administration.

As Saskatoon Land and administration prepared to work on the naming requests for the University Heights 3 neighborhood, a challenge arose. The current policy stated that naming comes in via requests. The approved Place Identity Framework recommends moving towards engaging with the community and residents on possible names. Given the policy has not been updated based on the requests from the Legacy Naming Project, this posed a challenge for administration on what direction to use. A situation like this has not occurred previously.

At the November 2025 CNC meeting, administration brought forward a request from the committee for guidance on how to proceed with naming. The request was in light of three factors: there are multiple neighborhood concept plans being developed and these neighborhoods would require names; Saskatoon Land had a pressing need for a name for the University Heights 3 neighborhood; and as I mentioned, the current approved naming policy and the more recently approved Place Identity Framework did not fully align in direction. At that time, Saskatoon Land also brought forward a request to add the name Hawthorne to the names master list. The committee resolved in that meeting to bring forward the Hawthorne name for consideration at the December 2025 meeting, as well as that any additional neighborhood names be considered under the new Place Identity Framework.

At the December 2025 CNC meeting, a report came forward with a request to add Hawthorne to the names master list and to be recommended as the name for the University Heights 3 neighborhood. During the December meeting, discussions were had regarding the alignment to the Place Identity Framework, specifically as it relates to engaging with the community on names for the UH3 neighborhood. The resolution from that meeting was to defer the recommendation related to Hawthorne to allow time for targeted and expedited community engagement, and that the targeted engagement be brought back to the CNC.

Based on the direction in December, administration engaged with the Indigenous community and other community members on a proposed name for the UH3 neighborhood. The engagement with the Indigenous community included ceremonial practices and was treated as an important part of the engagement and strengthening the alignment to the Place Identity Framework. There were valuable learnings that came from this engagement with the Indigenous community. It was learned that the name Hawthorne had ceremonial significance within the Indigenous community, and although this is a good name to add to the names list, it would be more appropriate to use for other spaces, as an example, maybe a name for a park. It was learned that "Sunrise" was a name that was most meaningful to not only the Indigenous community but other parts of our community. With the new neighborhood's eastward location and the connection to Indigenous teachings about the sun greeting the land, this name resonated strongly with those that were part of the process. Without this consultation, we may not have had these insights, and we are thankful for the support and engagement of those who participated in the engagement process.

As part of making the recommendation to the CNC in April, administration leveraged information from the November and December 2025 CNC reports, as well as the results of the engagement process. After collaboration across Saskatoon Land, Planning and Development, and other relevant departments, administration is requesting the following recommendation: The Civic Naming Committee recommend to the Standing Policy Committee on Planning, Development, and Community Services four items. First, that the proposed Hawthorne name be added to the names master list under the theme of flora and fauna. Second, that the proposed Sunrise name be added to the names master list under the theme of environment. Third, that the Sunrise name be applied to the University Heights 3 neighborhood. And fourth, that the report be forwarded to City Council for information.

With the current policy and Place Identity Framework not fully aligned, I'd like to discuss the approach to handling any new naming request before the policy is updated. For future name requests, and until the revisions to the policy are approved, the CNC and administration will need to ensure alignment with the currently approved policy. But as we've seen, if the CNC requested administration to align with the Place Identity Framework, a request for exception by the CNC would need to be made to PDCS and City Council. Additionally, revisions to the existing naming policy are currently being identified by administration. Recommended updates in alignment with the Place Identity Framework will be returned to the CNC within the next several months. Analysis of the options, including any resource or budget implications, will be provided when the report comes forward.

Thank you for your time. Myself and other members of administration are here to answer any questions you may have. I will open up for questions. Any questions?
Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Chair.
There are two things. First, thank you for the report. The work on this was done in collaboration with the community, in part through consultation. My question is about the name 'Court on' that's being added to the list. According to the report and the presentation, it was indicated that during the process, it has been identified as having some significant ceremonial Indigenous cultural importance. So, how is this name going to be used in the future?
Well, I'll call on one of my peers to speak to the significance of the name. But what I would say is when a name is added to the list, as requests come forward for new neighborhoods, parks, or other land items, we go through the list based on the theme area and the appropriateness of the name. Those would come forward to C&C through a process that's used by administration to recommend a particular name, which then would go on to this committee for approval. So, that's your question.
Yes, that answers it partially. The part that's probably not answered is the significance of the cultural aspect of it. How is that going to be applied in the future, and what would that entail? I just wanted to get an understanding.
I'll ask Dorothy to come forward and answer that, please.
Good morning again. So, when we're talking about that... I'm sorry, I'm just trying to find the right words for it. That's one of our traditional medicines, and that medicine is used in a very specific ceremony, right? So when we met about that name, we thought about where we would be having, say, ceremony, where we would find it. So, kind of like in a park area within the city, because it's natural, right? My name is Lenore Meyer. I'm the Executive and Artistic Director at the Broadway Theatre, situated in the heart of Broadway, here in Saskatoon. Thank you for the opportunity to speak about something that really matters, not just to our organization, but to the cultural and economic vitality of our community. I'm here to advocate for the impacts of the City of Saskatoon's tax abatement program as it applies to the Broadway Theatre and many other arts organizations in the city, and to highlight the meaningful, measurable impact that this support has had and continues to have on both our organization and the broader public. The Broadway Theatre is much more than a building. It's a community hub, a gathering space, and a platform for diverse voices. For decades, it has offered a stage for independent film, live music, local artists, dozens of festivals, and community events that would otherwise struggle to find a home. It contributes to the unique identity of Saskatoon, something that can't be replicated by large commercial venues or streaming platforms. Maintaining a historic non-profit arts venue also comes with a lot of real financial challenges, as well as rising operational costs and ongoing structural maintenance, all putting pressure on increasingly limited resources. This is where the city's tax abatement program plays a critical role for us, especially in a time when provincial public funding for the arts in our province has flatlined for over a decade. By easing the property tax burden, the program allows us to reinvest directly into programming, accessibility, staffing, and community outreach. Instead of diverting funds to cover fixed costs, we're able to maintain what we offer: more films, performances, more partnerships, and more opportunities for people in Saskatoon to connect through shared cultural experiences in the arts. The program's impact extends far beyond our walls. First, there's a clear economic benefit. The Broadway Theatre draws over 75,000 visitors each year through our doors and also through the Broadway district. These patrons also support the many nearby restaurants, cafes, and local businesses during their visits. A vibrant arts venue increases foot traffic, strengthens local commerce, and contributes to a more dynamic and resilient neighborhood economy. Second, there is also a social and cultural return. Our programming amplifies local voices, supports emerging artists, and creates inclusive spaces where people from all walks of life can come together. Whether it's a documentary screening, a live concert, or a community-led event, these experiences foster dialogue, understanding, and a stronger sense of belonging. Third, there is a long-term community investment. Cities that prioritize arts and culture are cities that attract talent, retain residents, and build pride among their citizens. Supporting institutions like the Broadway Theatre signals that Saskatoon values creativity, diversity, and community connection. The tax abatement program is not simply a financial concession; it is a strategic investment. It recognizes that organizations like ours generate returns that are not always captured on a balance sheet, but are deeply felt across the world. In an ever-changing industry that has become inherently volatile and unpredictable, the tax abatement we receive from the City of Saskatoon provides a major source of stable funding support that we now fully rely on as part of our operations. Without this support, we would most definitely face many difficult choices: reducing programming and staff, or limiting access. With it, we can continue to grow, innovate, and serve as a cultural cornerstone for Saskatoon. The benefits of the tax abatement program are clear: a stronger arts sector, a more vibrant local economy, and a more connected community. Thank you for your time and commitment to making Saskatoon a city where arts and culture thrive. Great. Thank you very much. Any questions for our speaker? Not seeing any. Thank you very much. Item 6.3.1. Miss Leslie Anderson, Director of Planning and Development, will introduce this report. Good morning. At the Governance and Priorities Committee in January, there was a request from Karen Kobasin, who is here today to answer any questions, on behalf of the Saskatoon West Business Association, indicating interest from the Association in establishing a new Business Improvement District for the Confederation Urban Center. That was referred to administration, report to which is before you today.

Establishment of a new Business Improvement District has not happened for some time; the last one was in 2013-2014 on 33rd Street. But it's guided by the Business Improvement Districts Bylaw, which was set up in 2022 as a newer, more modern version of that bylaw. So, it sets various requirements that apply to all the Business Improvement Districts in the city, and it also sets the process for establishment of a new district. Business Improvement Districts are funded through a levy that is paid for by operators of businesses in the area. The city collects that levy, but the levy is on top of their existing property taxes. It goes to the BID for their identified operations. Therefore, as part of this process, businesses will want to understand what services will be provided by the BID and what value it provides, as well as how much it will cost them, among other things.

So, engagement with the potential business operators in the area is an important part of establishing a new BID. At this time, the organizing committee has been provided with the information regarding what they need to do to establish a new BID. They've been given the assessment information to help them determine their budget and to identify the potential levy impacts to individual properties and businesses. They've been undertaking meetings to meet with the businesses and discuss their proposal. We've outlined the requirements for them for the process to move forward. There are basically two paths that can be taken to move this forward. One is that the organizing committee comes forward with a petition in support of establishing the BID. The petition has to meet certain thresholds: 50% of the operators of businesses in the area, and they have to represent 50% of the total taxable business assessment. They must be in support of the proposal and sign that petition for it to be brought forward.

The other option is that the city issues notices to all businesses in the proposed area. This would be a later process where the business owners could object in writing to the proposal. Those objections would come to the city. The written objections have to come from at least one-third of the operators of businesses in the area, and they have to represent at least one-third of the total taxable business assessment in the proposed area. If that threshold is met, then the city does not bring forward the proposed establishment to a public hearing. The organizers are pursuing the first path, so they are seeking support for their proposal. Once they've determined that they're ready to proceed, they'll indicate to us either that they have the resulting petition or that they have a change in direction. Then we will take forward our required actions to set up the required public hearing, issue notices, etc.

The resulting public hearing, if we get to that stage, means City Council still has the ultimate discretion to decide to approve or to object to the establishment of a new BID. City Council will take the time at the public hearing to understand whether there is support for that proposal to go ahead. We did note that there are some financial implications in the report. In general, the process of establishing a BID has some minor financial implications, with the most notable being the ongoing responsibility to collect the levy and distribute the funds to the BID. Establishing a new BID does not necessarily, or automatically, create a requirement for additional services or financial support from the city. We have five other existing BIDs, four of which receive an annual grant from the city, which is from parking meter funds.

The 33rd Street BID does not have paid parking in its area, nor does this proposed BID, so it would not be eligible for a similar grant. In addition, the city's urban design program is also largely funded by parking meter revenues, and its mandated area is limited to the four BIDs with paid parking. So, we would also not be expanding the services of the urban design program to this proposed area. If the BID proceeds, any future requests from the BID for any increased service levels or other area-specific projects would need to come through a request to committee and council and a potential budget option as well. So, at this time, as I noted, the organizing committee is working on their end to engage with businesses in the area. Once they indicate readiness for next steps to us, then we will bring forward any required components of the work. And Ms. Kobasin is here to answer any questions of committee if you have any.

We will go to 6.2.4, Vacant Lot and Adaptive Reuse Incentives. I believe we have comments from Prolog Development available for any questions, along with Nathan Evans and Action Group of Companies. Melissa Austin, Neighborhood Planning Manager, will introduce this report. "Good morning, committee. Thank you for the introduction."

This report includes two applications for development incentives under the Vacant Lot and Adaptive Reuse Incentive Program. The first application, outlined in the report, is from Action Group of Companies, requesting a five-year incremental property tax abatement for the development of five lots on the 400 block of Third Avenue North in the City Park neighborhood, just north of 25th Street. The project is a six-story rental apartment building with 83 residential units and 75 parking stalls. The applicants indicated a total investment of approximately $22 million. The project qualified for the maximum incentive, which is 100% of the incremental property taxes for a period of five years upon completion of the project. The estimated annual value of the abatement is approximately $160,000. The estimated five-year total abatement is approximately $810,000. The abatement for the subject property will begin the taxation year following the completion of the project, no later than January 1, 2030.

Incremental property tax abatement results in the deferral of the increased taxes that new construction creates. After the abatement period, the full increased assessment values are added to the tax base on an ongoing basis. The second application, outlined in the report, is a request for a one-time grant incentive for the adaptive reuse at 324 24th Street West, located in Caswell Hill. The existing building on this site may be familiar as it is the former Saskatoon Transit maintenance building and has been vacant since 2017 when transit operations were relocated to the Civic Operations Centre. This redevelopment will contain a variety of uses, including a community performance theater, artists' studios, restaurant, and retail space. The applicant indicated their total investment in this project is estimated to be about $5 million. Development incentives provided under the Vacant Lot program are based upon the incremental property taxes generated from pre-construction to post-construction of the project. Following review by Corporate Revenue, the planned redevelopment of the existing building is not anticipated to generate that incremental tax. This is not uncommon for adaptive reuse projects because the existing taxes prior to redevelopment would be higher compared to a project built on a vacant lot itself, where the taxes are lower. The program policy acknowledges this situation. In these situations where projects don't incur a tax increment upon completion, they can receive a grant equal to one year's worth of property taxes.

The estimated maximum value of this grant will be approximately $40,000, which does include the municipal and library tax portions. The actual value of the grant will be determined upon completion of the project and further assessment, and will be based on the project's eligibility using the Vacant Lot program's evaluation system. The grant will be paid out once the adaptive reuse project is complete and the associated annual property taxes are finalized.
